reason: The run renders the one core sense, paying or giving back what is owed or deserved, in several ways: "repay" (Matt 18; Rom 2:6), "pay back" (Matt 5:26; Luke 12:59; 19:8; Rev 18:6), "pay" (Rom 13:7), "give" (1 Cor 7:3; Matt 21:41) and "give back" (the Caesar saying). It also departs from tradition without a note in Matt 6:4, 6, 18 ("repay" for "reward") and with a note in the Caesar saying ("give back" for "render"). The Caesar saying is consistent across the three Synoptics here, but only by chance, since each chapter is translated separately. The other variation (sell, yield, give an account) reflects genuinely different senses and is fine.
sense: To pay or give back what is owed or deserved: debts, dues, and recompense for conduct, good or bad. This is the core active sense; the entry does not govern the middle voice (sell) or the idioms listed in the alternates.

alternates.when: What is owed is not the return of something received, so that 'repay' would be wrong in English: wages, taxes and dues (Matt 20:8; Rom 13:7).

Returning a thing or person to the one it came from or belongs to (Luke 4:20; 9:42). Also use 'give back' in the Caesar saying in all three Synoptics (Matt 22:21; Mark 12:17; Luke 20:25), where the verb answers the questioners' simple 'give' and treats the coin as already Caesar's.

What is due is not money and English says neither 'repay' nor 'pay': produce due to a landlord (Matt 21:41), the marital due (1 Cor 7:3), a body released to the one who asked for it (Matt 27:58), testimony the apostles were charged to give (Acts 4:33).
With λόγον as object: answering for one's conduct or management (Matt 12:36; Luke 16:2; Acts 19:40; Heb 13:17; 1 Pet 4:5).
With oaths or vows as object (Matt 5:33).
The object is a prize or crown given by a judge (2 Tim 4:8).
The subject is a tree, or discipline pictured as bearing fruit (Heb 12:11; Rev 22:2).

traditional: render (the Caesar saying, Rom 13:7 and 1 Cor 7:3 in the KJV line); also pay, reward, recompense, depending on context
rationale: In ordinary Koine, including commercial papyri and the Septuagint, this compound means handing over what is due: repaying a loan, paying a wage, or giving someone what their conduct has earned. "Repay" covers both debt and recompense in current English, works for good and bad outcomes alike, and is what the run already favours. "Render" no longer conveys the sense, and "reward" suits only good outcomes and blurs the verb with the separate noun for "reward" (μισθός) in the same passages.
standard_view: Lexicons agree on the sense (give back, pay what is due, recompense), and modern versions vary only in English wording. Most have "reward" in Matt 6:4, 6, 18 and "repay" or "render" in Matt 16:27 and Rom 2:6, so "repay" in Matthew 6 is a mild departure for consistency. In the Caesar saying the ESV and NASB keep "render", the NRSV and NET have "give", and the NIV has "give back"; some scholars prefer simply "pay", so "give back" there is an editorial choice within the accepted range.
